newsitem.title: USA: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Techs remain focus in slow trade.
newsitem.headline: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Techs remain focus in slow trade.

text.p: The usual technology names continued to dominate stock options activity in slow, listless post-expiration Monday trade, traders said.
They said it could take a few more days before activity picks up after February expirations last Friday.

The Dow Industrials had a fairly big rally, but even International Business Machines Corp and Philip Morris Cos Inc shares, whose big gains carried most of the load for the Dow, saw less options volume than usual, they noted.

"There's really nothing concentrating on any one issue," said Rod Jamieson, vice president of options strategy at EVEREN Securities. "There's just been more in tech stocks as usual, people kind of playing them for the bounces."

IBM March 145 calls topped the most actives list on the Chicago Board Options Exchange, but volume totalled only 3,991 contracts with less than half an hour to trade -- not very much compared with IBM's usual levels. Underlying stock was up 5-7/8 at 143-1/2 in late trade.
In Philip Morris options on the American Stock Exchange, March 130 calls were the busiest, with 2,698 lots trading.
The stock was up 6-1/4 at 135-1/4 in late trade on various speculations about the outcome of tobacco litigations and on positive technical outlook of the stock price, traders said.
U.S. Robotics Corp drew good interest as the company began shipping its long awaited x2 modems, which provide high-speed connection to the Internet.
Michael Schwartz, a managing director of Oppenheimer & Co, said call buyers had to chase rapidly receding offers when the stock began rising in early trade.
March 65.0 call was the heaviest traded on volume of 2,583 contracts, with the stock up 2-1/2 at 59-1/8.
Jamieson said U.S. Robotics had also seen some good interest in selling puts recently. But he said the stock had been falling steadily since December and might not be out of the woods yet.
Elsewhere, most of the heavily traded options owed their volume to large institutional orders, traders said.
